newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: European summit struggles on security disputes.
newsitem.headline: European summit struggles on security disputes.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

A European security summit, despite promising peace and cooperation in the 21st century, struggled on Tuesday with fresh arguments over the protests in Serbia and the problems of former Soviet republics.

Western diplomats said Russia, which has criticised NATO's plans for expanding into Eastern Europe, had insisted the summit's final declaration remove a call for democracy in Serbia, where President Slobodan Milosevic faces mass protests.

A long-running row between Armenia and Azerbaijan threatened to block the entire declaration, which promises security and stability for all in the new millennium. The document, which has to be agreed by all countries, was supposed to be issued later on Tuesday at the end of the two-day meeting.

Differences between Russia and NATO and the crisis in Belarus had overshadowed the first day of the summit, which has brought together leaders from more than 50 nations in the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

"As we approach the new century, it is more important than ever that we build together a peaceful...region where all our nations and individuals feel secure," the leaders said in a draft version of the final declaration.

"We are determined to learn from the tragedies of the past and to translate our vision of a cooperative future into reality by creating a common security space free of dividing lines in which all states are equal partners."

Many leaders have expressed concern that Serbia's Milosevic, facing an unprecedented challenge to his nine years of autocratic rule, could use force against protesters now thronging the streets of Belgrade and calling on him to quit.
Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, did not attend the summit because its OSCE membership has been suspended.

But Russia, which has often taken Serbia's side in the Yugoslav conflict, appeared ready to flex its diplomatic muscles in support of Milosevic after Western countries ignored Moscow's pleas on NATO expansion.
Western diplomats said Russia insisted a phrase from the draft declaration calling for "democratisation, independent media, free and fair elections" in Serbia was removed.
"The Russians have been insistent and eloquent defenders of the unfortunate Yugoslav poisition," said one diplomat.
Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin had told the summit on Monday that Moscow still opposed NATO plans to take in countries such as Poland and Hungary by the year 2000.

Russia won little support at the summit for strengthening the OSCE as a counterbalance to NATO but Moscow did win agreement on a new round of arms control talks that would adapt and extend a Cold War-era arms agreement on conventional forces.

The dispute which could torpedo the final summit declaration was played out on the fringes of the summit by Armenia and Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, an enclave which has an Armenian majority but is surrounded by Azeri territory.
Azerbaijan wants its territorial integrity reaffirmed in the final document, but Armenia is opposed to such a reference.

Either Armenia or Azerbaijan could block the final communique because every OSCE member has the right to a veto. Diplomats said efforts to resolve the dispute continued on Tuesday, but there was little sign of progress.
The last major European security summit, in Budapest in 1994, collapsed in humiliating disarray after a row on the NATO issue and differences over the war in Bosnia.
The disputes in Lisbon, although serious, are not as bitter or threatening -- principally because the war in Bosnia ended last year.
The summit declaration will also approve a continued role for the OSCE in Bosnia next year, working alongside the NATO-led peace force and supervising local elections.
The OSCE's Bosnia operation builds on its role as a monitor of democracy, human rights and arms control. The forum has its roots in a 1975 East-West conference in Helsinki.
In other developments on Tuesday, Germany and the Czech Republic said they were hopeful a dispute over ethnic Germans expelled from part of Czechoslovakia after World War Two would be solved soon.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl met Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus on the margins of the summit.
